\chapter{Welcoming a Guest}
\label{ch:sa-welcome}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the five steps of a Sanskrit welcome, from the door to the hands that make the greeting.}

Complete SA-C30-anjali and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dvāram]{\sk{द्वारम्} (dvāram) — a door, a gate}

\label{lesson:SA-C30-door}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dhanyaḥ} mean, and what was inside \emph{dhanyavādaḥ}?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{द्वारम्}}
\textbf{\sk{द्वारम्}} (\emph{dvāram}) — \textquotedblleft{}a door, a gate\textquotedblright{}.

A guest is met at the \textbf{\sk{द्वारम्}} — the door, the gate.

This is one of the securest cousins in the book. Latin \emph{foris} and \emph{forēs}, \textquotedblleft{}door\textquotedblright{} — whence \emph{forum}, the space outside the door, and \emph{foreign}, what is out of doors. Greek \emph{thura}. English \emph{door}, German \emph{Tür}, Russian \emph{dver}. The word for the opening of a house survived every migration intact, which is what you would expect of a word every generation says every day. Indian place names keep it too: \emph{Haridwar} is Hari's gate.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A door, and a word that reached every branch of the family.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dvāram}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dvāram}, and name two of its cousins outside India
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{द्वारम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a door, a gate\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āsanam]{\sk{आसनम्} (āsanam) — a seat}

\label{lesson:SA-C30-seat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{dvāram} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{आसनम्}}
\textbf{\sk{आसनम्}} (\emph{āsanam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a seat\textquotedblright{}.

Having met the guest at the door, you offer an \textbf{\sk{आसनम्}} — a seat. The root means \textquotedblleft{}to sit\textquotedblright{}, and the ending makes it the thing you sit on.

English borrowed the word without the furniture: an \emph{āsana} in yoga is a posture, a way of being seated. Both senses live in the one Sanskrit word, and the ordinary one is the older. Neuter \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}, like \sk{द्वारम्} before it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second step of a welcome, and a third borrowed word restored.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āsanam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dvāram}, then \emph{āsanam}, in the order a guest meets them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{आसनम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a seat\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puṣpam]{\sk{पुष्पम्} (puṣpam) — a flower}

\label{lesson:SA-C30-flower}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{āsanam} mean, and what did \emph{dvāram} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पुष्पम्}}
\textbf{\sk{पुष्पम्}} (\emph{puṣpam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{पुष्पम्}} is a flower. Its root means \textquotedblleft{}to bloom, to thrive, to nourish\textquotedblright{}, so the word names the opening rather than the petals.

You already have \textbf{\sk{फलम्}}, the fruit, and now the flower that precedes it — and in Sanskrit the pair \emph{puṣpa-phala} travels together as a set phrase, flower-and-fruit, the way English says \emph{bricks and mortar}. Neuter \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}, like \sk{फलम्} itself.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A flower to set beside the fruit you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puṣpam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{puṣpam}, then \emph{phalam}, and say them as one pair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{पुष्पम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mālā]{\sk{माला} (mālā) — a garland}

\label{lesson:SA-C30-garland}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{puṣpam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{माला}}
\textbf{\sk{माला}} (\emph{mālā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a garland\textquotedblright{}.

Threaded, the flowers become a \textbf{\sk{माला}} — a garland, put over the head of a guest of honour, and also the string of beads counted through in prayer. English borrowed the second sense as \emph{mala}.

Its own history is unsettled: no agreed cousin outside India, like \sk{केशः} and \sk{अलम्} before it. Feminine, ending in \textbf{-\sk{आ}}, like \sk{यात्रा} and \sk{माता}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A third word with no proven travels, and a garland made of the last one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mālā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{puṣpam}, then \emph{mālā}, and name what turns one into the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{माला} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a garland\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[añjaliḥ]{\sk{अञ्जलिः} (añjaliḥ) — the two hands cupped together}

\label{lesson:SA-C30-anjali}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{mālā} mean, and what did \emph{dvāram} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अञ्जलिः}}
\textbf{\sk{अञ्जलिः}} (\emph{añjaliḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the two hands cupped together\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{अञ्जलिः}} is the two hands brought together, palms cupped — the gesture your hands make when you say \textbf{\sk{नमस्ते}}.

The root means \textquotedblleft{}to anoint, to smear\textquotedblright{}, and the cupped hands were first of all a vessel: the shape you make to carry water, or an offering. The gesture of greeting began as the shape of giving something away. So the welcome closes where the book opened, on the first word you learned, with the hands finally named.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five steps of a welcome — door, seat, flower, garland, and the hands themselves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{añjaliḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say \emph{namaste} and name what your hands are doing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{अञ्जलिः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the two hands cupped together\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
